analysis.one_liner: Makes foreign oil cartels like OPEC subject to U.S. antitrust lawsuits for price-fixing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The NOPEC Act would amend U.S. antitrust law to make it illegal for foreign states, such as members of OPEC, to act together to limit oil production or set prices in ways that affect the American market. It would strip those foreign states of the sovereign immunity that normally protects them from U.S. lawsuits, and give the Justice Department sole power to sue them. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers of gasoline, heating oil, and natural gas would benefit if the bill passed, since a legal deterrent to foreign price-fixing could lower energy prices. U.S. oil and gas producers could also gain market share if foreign cartel output restrictions were deterred.

how_it_helps.text: It declares it illegal for foreign states to act collectively to limit oil and gas production or set prices when that affects the U.S. market, effectively making OPEC-style coordination subject to U.S. antitrust law.

It removes the sovereign-immunity shield foreign states normally rely on in U.S. courts and lets the Attorney General sue them, so cartel pricing that raises gasoline, heating, and electricity costs could be challenged in court.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign oil-producing states (OPEC members) could face antitrust judgments, and there is a risk of retaliation against U.S. interests abroad. Energy price volatility could also rise in the short term.

drawbacks.text: Removing sovereign immunity could expose foreign governments to sweeping U.S. lawsuits, which critics warn could invite retaliation against the United States and complicate energy and diplomatic relationships.
Enforcement is left solely to the Attorney General, so the bill's real-world effect would depend entirely on each administration's willingness to sue oil-producing states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a legal deterrent to foreign oil cartels — was never tested because the bill died. The drawbacks are real: subjecting foreign states to U.S. court judgments could invite retaliation against U.S. companies and diplomats abroad, and prior versions of the idea drew objections from defense and diplomatic agencies. On paper the consumer benefit outweighs those risks, but the bill never received even a committee hearing, so its design was never examined in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Buck introduced the bill on May 5, 2023, with Reps. Nadler and Cicilline as original sponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign oil-producing states keep their immunity from U.S. antitrust suits, and no cartel-pricing lawsuits can proceed. American drivers and consumers are left with no new legal tool against OPEC-style price coordination.

for.name: Rep. Ken Buck
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expose foreign oil cartels to U.S. antitrust suits.

for.name: Reps. Jerrold Nadler and David Cicilline

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after it was referred on May 5, 2023.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican (Buck) introduced the bill with two Democratic cosponsors, and the three listed cosponsors were Democrats [S4] — the bill itself was bipartisan, though the record shows no floor action to divide by party.

industries.industry: State-owned oil exporters (OPEC and OPEC+ members)
industries.note: The bill would make their coordinated production and pricing decisions legally actionable in U.S. courts and strip their sovereign immunity. Every prior NOPEC version died without becoming law.

Higher prices from foreign cartels currently lift U.S. producers' revenues; an antitrust check on cartel pricing could lower prices and their margins. The bill applies only to foreign states, not to domestic companies.
